title: Explain the common microservices design patterns (API Gateway, Service Discovery, Circuit Breaker, Saga, Event Sourcing, CQRS, Strangler Fig, Database per Service, Sidecar, Bulkhead).

s1_definition.profdef: Microservices patterns are reusable solutions to recurring distributed-system problems. API Gateway is a single entry point for routing and cross-cutting concerns. Service Discovery lets services find each other dynamically. Circuit Breaker stops cascading failures by failing fast. Saga manages distributed transactions with compensations. Event Sourcing stores state as an append-only log of events. CQRS separates the write model from the read model. Strangler Fig migrates a monolith incrementally. Database-per-Service gives each service a private store. Sidecar co-deploys helper functionality beside a service. Bulkhead isolates resource pools so one failure cannot sink everything.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, API Gateway is the reception desk. Service Discovery is the campus directory. Circuit Breaker is the "counter closed" sign. Saga is the undo process when a two-step transfer half-fails. Event Sourcing is the passbook that records every transaction instead of only the final balance. CQRS is having a fast "balance display screen" separate from the slow "ledger writing desk". Strangler Fig is renovating the old bank one department at a time while it stays open. Bulkhead is keeping the loan queue and the transfer queue in separate rooms so a loan rush does not block transfers.
s1_definition.oneliner: Gateway routes, Discovery finds, Circuit Breaker protects, Saga compensates, Event Sourcing logs, CQRS splits read/write, Strangler Fig migrates, DB-per-service isolates data, Sidecar helps, Bulkhead contains failure.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Microservices patterns are reusable solutions to recurring distributed-system problems. API Gateway is a single entry point for routing and cross-cutting concerns. Service Discovery lets services find each other dynamically. Circuit Breaker stops cascading failures by failing fast. Saga manages distributed transactions with compensations. Event Sourcing stores state as an append-only log of events. CQRS separates the write model from the read model. Strangler Fig migrates a monolith incrementally. Database-per-Service gives each service a private store. Sidecar co-deploys helper functionality beside a service. Bulkhead isolates resource pools so one failure cannot sink everything.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, API Gateway is the reception desk. Service Discovery is the campus directory. Circuit Breaker is the "counter closed" sign. Saga is the undo process when a two-step transfer half-fails. Event Sourcing is the passbook that records every transaction instead of only the final balance. CQRS is having a fast "balance display screen" separate from the slow "ledger writing desk". Strangler Fig is renovating the old bank one department at a time while it stays open. Bulkhead is keeping the loan queue and the transfer queue in separate rooms so a loan rush does not block transfers.

**One line to remember:** Gateway routes, Discovery finds, Circuit Breaker protects, Saga compensates, Event Sourcing logs, CQRS splits read/write, Strangler Fig migrates, DB-per-service isolates data, Sidecar helps, Bulkhead contains failure.

sections.s2_technical:
The API Gateway pattern puts one entry point in front of all services. In Spring Cloud Gateway you route `Path=/api/v1/payments/**` to `lb://payment-service` with filters for auth and rate limiting. Service Discovery pairs with it: services register under a logical name and callers resolve it, for example a Feign client `@FeignClient(name="account-service")` that the runtime maps to a live instance.

The Circuit Breaker pattern wraps a remote call, for example `@CircuitBreaker(name="accountService", fallbackMethod="fallback")`, moving CLOSED to OPEN to fail fast. The Bulkhead pattern limits concurrent calls to a dependency, for example `@Bulkhead(name="accountService")`, so a flood to one dependency cannot starve threads needed by others. The Saga pattern replaces two-phase commit: a payment saga debits then credits, and on failure runs a compensating `accountClient.credit(from, amount)`.

Event Sourcing stores every change as an immutable event, so instead of updating a balance column you append `AccountDebited` and `AccountCredited` events and rebuild the balance by replaying them. CQRS separates writes from reads: the command side appends events while a read model is projected for fast queries, for example a materialized `balance_view`. Database-per-Service keeps each service's store private, which is what makes Event Sourcing and CQRS feasible per service.

The Strangler Fig pattern migrates a monolith gradually: the gateway routes some paths to a new service while the rest still hit the monolith, and you move one capability at a time until the monolith is gone. The Sidecar pattern deploys a helper container beside each service for logging, proxying, or TLS, as in a service mesh like Istio with an Envoy sidecar. The senior-level nuance is to use the smallest pattern that solves your problem: Event Sourcing and CQRS add real complexity and are justified only when you need full audit history or very different read and write scaling.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is modernizing. Problem 1 — auditors demand the full history of every change to Rajesh's account, not just the current balance. This is exactly Event Sourcing: store each debit and credit as an immutable event and replay to get the balance. Problem 2 — the "show my balance" screen is hit thousands of times per second while writes are rare, and querying the event log every time is slow. This is exactly CQRS: keep a fast read view separate from the write log. Problem 3 — a sudden rush of loan applications must not block ordinary transfers. This is exactly the Bulkhead pattern: separate resource pools.

The mini-project builds an event-sourced `AccountEventStore` that appends `AccountEvent` records, a `BalanceProjection` (the CQRS read model) updated from those events, and a `BulkheadExecutor` that caps concurrency per operation type. A runnable demo applies a debit and a credit to Rajesh, rebuilds his balance by replay, reads it instantly from the projection, and shows transfers continuing while a loan surge is contained.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001) opening balance 1,000,000, then a 50,000 debit and a 20,000 credit.

Step 1: The demo seeds the CQRS read model with Rajesh's opening balance of 1,000,000. The event store is still empty.

Step 2: A `DEBITED 50000` event is appended to the event store. The event is immutable; nothing overwrites a balance column. The same event is also applied to the read-model projection, dropping the view to 950,000.

Step 3: A `CREDITED 20000` event is appended and applied to the projection, raising the view to 970,000.

Step 4: To prove the event log is the source of truth, the demo replays all of Rajesh's events from the opening balance and recomputes 1,000,000 minus 50,000 plus 20,000 equals 970,000, matching the projection exactly.

Step 5: The bulkhead caps transfer concurrency at two permits. The first two transfers acquire permits and run; the third finds no permit and is shed, protecting the shared pool so a surge cannot starve other work.

```text
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:20 INFO === Event Sourcing: append debit + credit for Rajesh ===

Oct 24, 2026 11:52:20 INFO Appended CREDITED 20000 for SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:20 INFO Replayed balance = 970000
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:20 INFO CQRS read model balance = 970000
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Command: debit SAV2001 Rs.50000
    │
    ▼
  WRITE SIDE (CQRS command)
    │ append event ──→ AccountEventStore [DEBITED 50000]  (immutable log)
    │                         │
    │                         │ event published
    │                         ▼
    │                   BalanceProjection.apply()
    │                         │ view: 1,000,000 → 950,000
    ▼                         ▼
  READ SIDE (CQRS query)   balance_view (fast)
    │ balanceOf("SAV2001") → 950,000 (instant, no replay)
    ▼
  Audit: replay all events from opening → 970,000 (source of truth)

  Bulkhead:  [transfers pool: 2 permits] ─ 3rd request shed ─→ protect others
             [loans pool: separate permits] ─ surge contained here only
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Microservices design patterns are reusable solutions to the recurring problems of distributed systems, and I group them by the problem they solve. For entry and discovery, the API Gateway gives one front door for routing and authentication, and Service Discovery lets services find each other by logical name instead of hardcoded addresses. For resilience, the Circuit Breaker fails fast when a dependency is down, and the Bulkhead isolates resource pools so a surge in one area cannot starve the rest.

For data and transactions, the Saga pattern replaces two-phase commit by running steps with compensating actions. In my banking work, a transfer saga debits Rajesh then credits Priya, and if the credit fails it re-credits Rajesh. Database-per-Service keeps each service's store private, which is the foundation that makes the next two patterns possible. Event Sourcing stores every change as an immutable event, so auditors at National Bank of India can see the full history of an account and I can rebuild any balance by replaying events. CQRS separates the write model from the read model, so the balance-display screen reads from a fast projection while the command side appends events.

For migration, the Strangler Fig pattern lets me move a monolith to microservices one capability at a time, with the gateway routing new paths to new services and the rest still hitting the monolith until it is gone. For deployment, the Sidecar pattern co-locates a helper container for TLS, logging, and tracing, which is exactly how a service mesh like Istio works with Envoy.

The judgment I always share is to use the smallest pattern that solves the problem. Event Sourcing and CQRS add real complexity, so I reach for them only when I genuinely need full audit history or very different read and write scaling. Reaching for every pattern on day one produces a system that is harder to operate than the monolith it replaced.
